On my right hand there were lines of fishing stakes, mysterious in their purpose, and on my left a group of barren islets lay upon a sea so still that it seemed solid. <break time="0.8s" /> My ship lay at anchor at the head of the Gulf of Siam, and the only other sign of human life was the masts of a ship anchored inside the islands, half hidden by the land. <break time="0.8s" /> Appointed to this command only a fortnight before, I was a stranger to the ship and, if all the truth must be told, somewhat of a stranger to myself. <break time="0.8s" /> Not only was I new to the ship, but her officers and crew had been together for eighteen months, so that I alone was the outsider on board, watched by every man. <break time="0.8s" /> On that first evening I wondered how far I should turn out faithful to that ideal conception of ones own personality which every man sets up for himself secretly. <break time="0.8s" /> Wishing to know my ship and, perhaps, to steady my own nerves, I did a thing unusual for a captain, sending all hands to rest and keeping the anchor watch myself. <break time="0.8s" /> Pacing the deck alone, I noticed that the rope side ladder, which should have been hauled in, had been left hanging over the side, and I went to pull it up. <break time="0.8s" /> But the ladder would not come, and, looking over the rail, I saw in the faint glow of the water a naked man, whose body seemed silvery and ghostly, holding the lowest rung.

When I told him quietly that I was the captain, the swimmer, after a pause, gave his name as Leggatt and climbed aboard, and I hurried below to fetch him a sleeping suit. <break time="0.8s" /> Dressed in grey stripes exactly like my own, he stood beside me in the dark, and it seemed to me that I was looking at my double, my second self, risen out of the sea. <break time="0.8s" /> He had been chief mate of the Sephora, the ship anchored inside the islands, and during a terrible gale he had quarrelled with an insolent sailor who refused to obey his orders. <break time="0.8s" /> At the height of the storm he set a reefed foresail that saved the ship, yet in the struggle a huge sea fell upon them, and when the two men were found, the sailor was dead. <break time="0.8s" /> Shut up in his cabin for weeks by his captain, he expected to be handed over to the law at the first port and to be tried for the death on shore. <break time="0.8s" /> Finding his door unlocked one evening, he had slipped into the sea and swum to the islands, and from there, seeing my riding light, he had made for it, resolved never to go back. <break time="0.8s" /> Not for a moment did I think of calling my officers, for something in his calm, low voice made me feel that his trouble might, in other circumstances, have been mine. <break time="0.8s" /> So I led him to my stateroom, an L shaped room whose inner part could not be seen from the door, and there, side by side, we whispered in the dark.

The next morning a boat came from the Sephora, and her captain, a thin, red whiskered man named Archbold, climbed aboard, saying that he had lost his chief mate. <break time="0.8s" /> Pretending to be a little hard of hearing, I made him repeat everything in a loud voice, for I wanted the hidden listener in my cabin to hear every word that passed between us. <break time="0.8s" /> Archbold told the story in his own way, never mentioning, as Leggatt had told me, that it was the mate, not he, whose order to set the foresail had saved the Sephora. <break time="0.8s" /> To show him that I had nothing to hide, I took him round the whole ship, opening even the door of my own stateroom, while my double stood silent in the inner corner. <break time="0.8s" /> Seven and thirty years he had been at sea, he declared, and never had he heard of such a thing happening in an English ship. <break time="0.8s" /> At last he left, unsatisfied, suggesting that the poor fellow must have drowned, and I watched his boat pull away with a relief so deep that my hands were trembling. <break time="0.8s" /> I knew well that, in the eyes of the law, Leggatt was a man who had taken a life, and that I, by hiding him, had become the secret sharer of his fate.
